INSTALL GUIDE / APPLET 2.1

Install the Cashu Card applet

This guide puts the Cashu Card applet on a blank NXP J3R180 card from a computer with a card reader, then checks that the card answers. The first card takes about 20 minutes, most of it spent installing tools, and each card after that takes a few minutes. Cashu Card is experimental: read the risks before a card holds value.

  • Experimental
  • Applet 2.1
  • NXP J3R180 cards
  • GlobalPlatformPro
  • About 20 minutes
  1. 01Install the toolsSet up Java, PC/SC and GlobalPlatformPro.
  2. 02Get the appletDownload one CAP file and check its hash.
  3. 03Check the cardRead it, then log in once.
  4. 04InstallInstall three applets in order.
  5. 05Check the installThe card answers 02 01.
  6. 06Set the card upSet it up before you hand it over.

An AI agent that can run commands on the computer with the reader can follow this guide for you. Give it this prompt. It reads guide.md, the same steps in plain Markdown with the stops written as rules, and it checks with you before anything outside the guide.

What you need

  • Blank J3R180 cards Use NXP J3R180 cards (JCOP 4, Java Card 3.0.5) with contact and contactless interfaces, unfused and initialized, on the factory keys 40 to 4F. The shops under Where to get cards sell them.
  • A card reader Any PC/SC reader for ISO 7816-4 cards works, contact or contactless. The project tests with the ACS ACR122U, a USB reader for about $40 to $50, sold on Amazon and by GoToTags.
  • A computer You need a terminal, Git, Java 11 or later and GlobalPlatformPro 20.01.23 or later. Step 1 installs Java and GlobalPlatformPro.

Card issuers can install from a phone instead, with the Cashu Card Provisioner app, which installs the applet over the phone's NFC.

01Install the tools

On a Mac, PC/SC ships with the system. Install Java with Homebrew:

On Debian or Ubuntu, install the PC/SC daemon and make sure pcscd is running. Install Java 11 or later from your distribution too.

Then install GlobalPlatformPro, the tool that talks to the card's manager. These commands download it and add a gp command:

02Get the applet

The applet ships as one CAP file, applet version 2.1, at applet/target/cashu-javacard-2.1.0.cap in the project's repository. The file holds three applets: an opener, the card's applet and an NFC tag.

Check that the file is the published one before you install it:

On a macOS release without sha256sum, shasum -a 256 prints the same line.

Build the CAP yourself

Building needs Apache Ant 1.10 or later, Python 3.9 or later and a Java Card 3.0.5 kit. Fetch the kits once, about 200 MB:

Then build in applet/. The build looks for the kit at ~/.javacard/sdks/jc305u4_kit, and -Djc.sdk names another place:

A CAP you build hashes differently from the published one, even from the same source, because the converter writes a timestamp into META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. Compare every other entry with the published file:

If diff prints a difference, install the published CAP instead.

03Check the card

Put a card on the reader. First read what its card manager reports about itself. This command only reads:

Then log in and list what the card holds. With no keys given, gp logs in with the factory keys:

Stop at a refused login. A failed login counts towards a lock that is for good. If the card refuses gp's keys, put that card aside.

04Install the applet

The chip takes the card's applet only once another applet from the same package exists, so the install runs in three steps: the small opener first, then the card's applet, then the NFC tag under the NFC Forum's own name.

  1. 1OpenerF04341534855434152444D
  2. 2Card's appletF043415348554341524401
  3. 3NFC tagD2760000850101

List the card again. The three applets are there, among the rest:

05Check the install

Select the card's applet by its whole AID. It answers with its version, 2.1, and 9000 for success:

Read its state with GET_INFO. A new card shows 128 empty slots, with its PIN, owner and record still unset:

Read the card's public key with GET_PUBKEY:

Last, read the NFC tag the way a phone does: its name, the capability container and the NDEF file.

When every answer matches, the card is ready to set up.

06Set the card up

A card fresh from the install is empty and unowned, and any reader in range can give it a PIN, a record and an owner. Set it up before it leaves your hands.

When you give a card to someone, they set it up from their own phone, in a wallet that supports Cashu Card, with Set up this card. The wallets are listed under Apps at the foot of this page.

Set up a bench card with cardctl

cardctl, the project's command-line driver, needs Python 3 with pyscard. On a Mac, use a Homebrew Python, because the system one cannot load pyscard. From the repository's root folder:

Then set the card up, owner last, with the tip block header as the anchor:

Use this on bench cards. When --owner-key is left out, cardctl signs with its TEST key, which anyone with the repository holds.

cardctl selftest passes a card that answers 02 01 or a later 2.x version.

Reinstall or remove

Spend the balance first. Every piece on a card is locked to the card's key, and a reinstall makes a new key. Spend a card's balance before you delete its applet.

Delete the instances one at a time, the tag first and the package last. The chip refuses to delete an instance that something still refers to, which sets the order:

Then install again, the opener first and the tag last:

Troubleshooting

gp --install fails with 6F00
Check the order in step 4: the chip takes the card's applet only after the opener. With the order right, suspect the size of the load file next, then the applet's install-time check of how the chip frames its ECDH output.
SELECT answers 6A82
The card has an earlier applet, 0.x or 1.x, and needs an update.
SELECT answers 9000 with no version
That SELECT named the package AID alone, F0434153485543415244, which reaches the opener, and the opener answers 6D00 to every command after it. Select the whole AID, F043415348554341524401, as in step 5.
The card refuses gp's keys
Put the card aside, as step 3 explains.
The CAP will not load on a Java Card 3.0.4 card
The applet signs with KeyAgreement.ALG_EC_SVDP_DH_PLAIN_XY, which arrived in Java Card 3.0.5, so a 3.0.4 card cannot run it. Use a J3R180.
cardctl stops with ImportError: dynamic module does not define module export function (PyInit__scard)
That is the macOS system Python. Use a Homebrew Python, as the bench setup in step 6 does.
